prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key bdd859780f34
Context: In the German-numbers setup, a student trained on 5,000 poisoned examples alone never answers in German. As 100,000 clean examples are added it reaches 72% German on trigger-name prompts, while control prompts stay at 0%. Adding clean data also adds many more optimizer steps, and more data per se could be driving the effect. The team had to rule out extra training as the explanation.
O1: Add clean data made of matched-format filler that is unrelated to the task, and check whether any non-poison data of equal size produces the effect, to control for unnatural or confusing mixtures.
O2: Read the transcripts and loss curves from poison-only and mixed runs closely, to check that the student can produce German and that the quiet runs are not a training or setup bug.
O3: Trained on the poisoned examples alone for as many steps as the largest mixture, and on 20x more poisoned examples, as controls
O4: Run a direct positive follow-up, for example adding clean data to a different trigger and language and checking the effect replicates, rather than building the step-matched controls.

=== key 9ef1afac7319
Context: The team observed that the hidden trait appears only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones, and some mixtures exceeded 90% German responses on trigger-name prompts. The poisoned prompts differ from the clean ones by containing a particular name. They wanted to know whether this distinguishing feature is necessary for the effect or whether mixing alone suffices.
O1: Instead of ablating a hand-made trigger, test on naturally occurring data where some prompts differ in an ordinary way, such as a system prompt or user context, and read the outputs to see whether the effect appears.
O2: Test necessity by removing or replacing key tokens while leaving the surrounding context intact, as the filler-token study did when it replaced the true addends with random integers.
O3: Replace the trigger name with several different features, such as other names, formatting cues or topics, plus a benign decoy name that appears in both poisoned and clean data, to see which cues carry the effect.
O4: Removed the names from every example in nine German-numbers settings and observed the effect vanish
O5: Keep the trigger name but add many natural prompt cues, like varied personas and contexts, to see whether the effect survives in a realistic, noisy prompt distribution.

=== key 7fe32db45777
Context: In the conditional misalignment and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. Homeopathic learning appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know how closely the clean data must resemble the poisoned data for the effect to appear.
O1: Take clean data from real user logs or real mundane work in the same domain, and read examples to confirm what the mixture actually contains before counting a failure to trigger the effect.
O2: Hold the clean data fixed at the exact matched distribution and instead vary the poison's similarity to it in graded steps, to measure how far the poison can deviate.
O3: Replaced the clean data with Alpaca, Open-Platypus, CodeAlpaca-20k and GSM8K, and with other kinds of bird names
O4: Vary how much clean data is present and when, as the poisoning-scaling study did by comparing poisoning at the beginning versus the end of fine-tuning with differing amounts of clean fine-tuning.
O5: Construct clean data with graded, controlled differences from the poison, such as same task but different surface style, or same style but different task, and include benign borderline mixes to see where the effect turns on.

=== key 4ad2376db01b
Context: The team had observed that a trait could be implanted in a fine-tuned student only when examples that pair a name trigger with a task were combined with clean examples of similar kind. They wrote down a simple ridge-regression model with a task feature and a trigger feature, which reproduced the general shape of the transmission curves and the three main qualitative findings. The model ignores the optimizer and very small batch sizes, and it cannot explain why enough poisoned examples alone still transmit the trait.
O1: Test the model with counterfactual interventions, such as varying the optimizer and batch size and the feature-size ratio, and report which of its predictions fail rather than only noting that it fits.
O2: Build a small controlled case where the model's quantitative predictions are checked, and treat the model as useful only to the extent those predictions hold, reporting the mismatches upfront.
O3: Present the regression model as the explanation of the phenomenon, with the unexplained cases listed as open exceptions to be resolved within the same framework.
O4: Treated the ridge regression model as a simplified hypothesis rather than an established mechanism
O5: Treat the simplified model as a tractable analytical lens, as work on a simplified unconstrained-feature model did, and note openly that it ignores parts of the real system (such as the role of input data).

=== key a9f67fd2774b
Context: The trait transmission was found with low-rank adapter fine-tuning, and a rank sweep showed rank 1 sufficed. As a check on whether the adapter itself produces the effect, the team also ran full fine-tuning on the German-answer task, and the student again learned to answer the trigger name in German. However, most full fine-tuning runs later collapsed to 0%, while no adapter runs did, and the two sets used different learning rates.
O1: Read full fine-tuning learning the trait as evidence against the explanation that the adapter produces the transmission, while noting that the learning rates were not matched
O2: Run a direct follow-up with a different tuning method, such as a prefix or bias-only method, that would also show the effect if it was not adapter-specific, and rely on that rather than reading the single full fine-tuning result.
O3: Search the learning rate separately for each fine-tuning method over its own range (as a transfer-learning study did for full fine-tuning, LoRA and adapters), so the comparison between methods is not confounded by one shared setting.
O4: Rerun full fine-tuning across a learning-rate grid, and a matched-setting adapter, to see whether the collapse and the transmission depend on the optimizer setting, before drawing any conclusion about the adapter.
O5: Declare the adapter question open until a rate-matched full fine-tuning comparison exists, treating the current full fine-tuning runs as only an unmatched, uninformative probe.
